Hubert's influence can be traced through names, institutions, and images even where the history of the original burial has become uncertain.
hubert.reflection: Trace Maastricht, Liège, and Saint-Hubert on a map, distinguishing places in Hubert's ministry from the later destination of his remains.

hugh-of-grenoble.title: Making a way of life transferable
paragraphs: Hugh's encouragement helped Guigo, the fifth prior of Chartreuse, put the community's customs into writing, completed in 1127. The Carthusian Order's history connects that work with requests from other communities wishing to follow the same life. Writing allowed a practice learned in one place to be communicated beyond its original members.

Its later use among women makes the consequence concrete. In the mid-twelfth century, the nuns of Prébayon sought affiliation with the Carthusians and received the Customs through John of Spain. Hugh did not personally found this later branch; the connection is the institutional resource he had helped encourage. The text gave later communities something they could study, adopt, and gradually adapt.

sources.title: Carthusian Order: History of the nuns and origins

hugh-of-grenoble.reflection: Compare an unwritten community custom with a written rule that another house can receive. Use the path from Guigo to Prébayon to discuss the gains and difficulties of transmission.

hyacinth.title: A religious order traveling through communities
paragraphs: The traditional account of Hyacinth's journey north includes the foundation of a Dominican community at Friesach in Carinthia. This gives a useful intermediate setting between Rome and Poland: the spread of the order involved establishing places where friars could live together, rather than simply tracing the movements of one celebrated preacher.

His reception of the habit at Santa Sabina is likewise an institutional detail worth separating from later claims about extraordinarily distant journeys. Formation, profession, and the sending of a small group provided a structure for preaching. These stages help explain how a new religious order could extend its work while retaining relationships of common life and responsibility.
hyacinth.reflection: Map the Rome–Friesach–Poland route in the traditional account. Explain what founding a stable community adds to a traveling preacher's visit.

hyginus.title: Recognizing a formula in a later biography
paragraphs: One reason for caution about Hyginus's supposed reorganization of the clergy is unusually specific: the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the same general statement also appears in the biography of Pope Hormisdas, who lived much later. Repeated administrative language may function as a biographer's formula rather than preserve a distinctive second-century event.

This comparison offers a practical way to read sparse early papal records. Instead of expanding a repeated phrase into invented offices, ceremonies, or decrees, a reader can examine where else it occurs and how early the account is. Hyginus's place in succession remains a separate question from the reliability of that particular claim.
hyginus.reflection: Compare the administrative statement attributed to Hyginus with its parallel in Hormisdas's biography. Discuss what repetition can reveal about a compiler's methods.

ignatius-of-antioch.title: The people carrying the letters
paragraphs: The closing chapters of Ignatius's letter to the Smyrnaeans reveal the human network around a prisoner. He thanks the community for receiving Philo and Rheus Agathopus and names Burrhus as a companion through whom he writes from Troas. Such acknowledgments show that his letters depended on travelers, hospitality, and assistance.

He also asks the Smyrnaeans to choose a delegate to visit the church in Syria, now reported to be at peace. The request turns sympathy into a concrete act of interchurch communication. Read beside his better-known theological passages, these practical details reveal how unity was maintained through people willing to carry news, letters, and encouragement across distances.

sources.title: Ignatius of Antioch: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapters 10–12

ignatius-of-antioch.reflection: List the named helpers in chapters 10–12 of the Smyrnaeans letter and reconstruct their different roles in sustaining communication.

ignatius-of-loyola.title: A manual for guiding another person's prayer
paragraphs: The Spiritual Exercises were designed as directions for the person accompanying a retreatant, rather than simply a book to read straight through alone. The Jesuit Conference describes four periods moving through sin and mercy, Christ's life and call, his suffering and death, and resurrection and mission. Their sequence gives structure to discernment through sustained prayer.

The full retreat is commonly made over thirty days, but the tradition also includes the Exercises in Daily Life, known as the nineteenth-annotation retreat, and shorter adaptations. These forms show the difference between a spiritual method and one fixed timetable. Ignatius's legacy includes a practice that requires attention to the person receiving it and the circumstances in which prayer is possible.

sources.title: Jesuit Conference: The Spiritual Exercises of Saint Ignatius

ignatius-of-loyola.reflection: Compare a residential thirty-day retreat with the Exercises in Daily Life. Identify the different arrangements each requires for prayer, accompaniment, and ordinary responsibilities.

imelda-lambertini.title: A medieval story in modern catechesis
paragraphs: The English Dominican account of Blessed Imelda begins with a modern First Communion class in Oxford. Its author describes children reflecting on a period of Eucharistic adoration before turning to Imelda's traditional story. That framing is evidence for her continuing educational use, even though it is not an independent medieval witness to the miraculous events.

The same account locates her burial tradition at San Sigismondo in Bologna. Together, the remembered place and the catechetical example show two routes through which a brief life has endured: local veneration and repeated retelling for children. A careful presentation can explore reverence and desire while making clear which details belong to tradition and which describe modern teaching.
imelda-lambertini.reflection: Design a short First Communion discussion using Imelda's story, with one question about Eucharistic reverence and one sentence clearly identifying its miraculous elements as traditional.

irenaeus-of-lyon.title: A teacher of unity across East and West
paragraphs: On January 21, 2022, Pope Francis declared Irenaeus a Doctor of the Church with the title Doctor unitatis, or Doctor of Unity. The decree emphasizes the geographical shape of his life: a Christian formed in the East exercised episcopal ministry in the West. That movement made him a useful figure for reflecting on a shared Christian inheritance.

The document also connects his name with peace and expresses the hope that his teaching will support the search for full communion among Christians. This is a modern reception of Irenaeus's work, not an additional event in his ancient biography. It shows how a second-century author's concern for common faith can acquire fresh significance within later divisions.

sources.title: Pope Francis: Decree declaring Irenaeus Doctor of Unity, 2022

irenaeus-of-lyon.reflection: Read the short 2022 decree and identify why it emphasizes Irenaeus's East–West journey. Compare that purpose with the concerns of his own second-century writings.

isaac-jogues.title: The support and limits of a traveling mission
paragraphs: Jogues's first journey from Quebec to the Wendat settlement of Ihonatiria required nineteen days of paddling and carrying canoes around obstacles, according to the Jesuit account. The route depended on Indigenous companions and their knowledge. Those practical conditions belong within mission history as much as the actions of the European priest.

The same account records an invitation from a Chippewa group in 1641 that could not be followed by a permanent new mission because too few Jesuits were available. It also identifies René Goupil as a surgeon and Jean de La Lande as an experienced woodsman. Such details reveal requests, staffing limits, and specialized skills behind a narrative often reduced to captivity and death.
isaac-jogues.reflection: Outline the people and skills needed for Jogues's nineteen-day journey. Discuss how local invitations and limited personnel shaped where missionary work could proceed.

isidore-bakanja.title: Witnesses who interrupted concealment
paragraphs: A Carmelite account describes an attempt to remove the injured Bakanja from view when an inspector was due to visit. Bakanja reached the inspector, who intervened and arranged care. This episode adds an institutional dimension to his suffering: abuse depended partly on keeping a vulnerable worker beyond the notice of someone able to challenge it.

The account also records visits from two missionaries, who gave him the sacraments and heard his response about forgiving his aggressor. Their presence helps explain how his final months entered the surviving religious narrative. Reading those witnesses alongside the inspector's intervention keeps practical aid, testimony, and Bakanja's own convictions within the same history.
isidore-bakanja.reflection: Identify the different responsibilities of the inspector and the visiting missionaries in the Carmelite account. Discuss why witnessing abuse and providing care are both necessary.

isidore-of-seville.title: Collecting across cultural boundaries
paragraphs: Benedict XVI describes Isidore's learning through the idea of collatio: gathering and comparing inherited material. His intellectual range could move between Martial and Augustine, or Cicero and Gregory the Great. This explains both the richness of his compilations and their unevenness. Preservation sometimes mattered more than producing a perfectly integrated argument.

Isidore's approach therefore raises a concrete question about cultural transmission. A Christian scholar could regard works from pagan antiquity as worth saving and using, while still judging them through his own faith. His collections reveal an effort to retain what earlier generations had learned, even when the material did not originate within his religious community.
isidore-of-seville.reflection: Choose a short entry from the Etymologies and identify the kinds of knowledge it gathers. Discuss what a compiler preserves and what can be lost when material is removed from its earlier context.

isidore-the-farmer.title: From a parish life to a literary afterlife
paragraphs: The Catholic Encyclopedia identifies an important stage in Isidore's written tradition: a life composed in 1265 and supplemented in 1275 by John, a deacon of Madrid's church of Saint Andrew. Giving the writer and dates makes the distance from Isidore's lifetime concrete, rather than leaving the reader with an unspecified appeal to tradition.

That medieval life later supplied material for Lope de Vega's religious poem San Isidro, published in 1599. The movement from parish remembrance to a major literary work helps explain the laborer's wider cultural presence. It also requires care: a poet's elaboration may be valuable evidence for devotion and imagination without adding independent testimony about twelfth-century events.
isidore-the-farmer.reflection: Compare the dates of Isidore's life, the deacon John's account, and Lope de Vega's poem. Explain how the same story serves different audiences at each stage.

jacinta-marto.title: The route of her burial and remembrance
paragraphs: Jacinta's first resting place was in Ourém, where her remains stayed for fifteen years. The Shrine of Fátima records their transfer to Fátima's cemetery on September 12, 1935, and later to the basilica on April 30, 1951. These dates belong to the history of her public remembrance, distinct from the events of 1917.

A memorial at the Ourém cemetery was planned to mark that earlier burial place for local residents and pilgrims. Such a marker preserves a location that a visitor concentrating only on the present shrine could overlook. It makes the development of devotion visible as a sequence of places, decisions, and acts of remembrance rather than a single timeless setting.

sources.title: Shrine of Fátima: Memorial to Jacinta in Ourém

jacinta-marto.reflection: Draw Jacinta's burial itinerary from Ourém to the Fátima cemetery and basilica. Discuss why a community might preserve a memorial after the remains have moved.

jadwiga-of-poland.title: Royal resources for learning and care
paragraphs: In his canonization homily, John Paul II recalled Jadwiga's gift of a golden scepter to support the university, with a gilded wooden one used in its place. He treated the exchange as an image of authority directed toward education. The detail gives a tangible form to the connection between her royal position and the future of learning in Krakow.

The same homily names hospitals at Biecz, Sandomierz, Sącz, and Stradom among her works of mercy. Education and care for bodily needs appear together in this interpretation of her reign. The public legacy attributed to her therefore concerns several institutions with different tasks, rather than patronage of a university alone.

sources.title: John Paul II: Canonization homily for Queen Jadwiga, 1997

jadwiga-of-poland.reflection: Compare the purposes of Jadwiga's university support and the hospitals named in the canonization homily. Discuss how allocating royal wealth could serve both long-term learning and immediate need.

james-the-greater.title: The request for honor and the lesson of service
paragraphs: Benedict XVI's catechesis draws attention to a less comfortable part of James's discipleship: the request that he and his brother receive privileged places beside Jesus in the kingdom. Read alongside the later martyrdom notice, that episode prevents a portrait in which the apostle understood the meaning of following Christ completely from the beginning.

The catechesis interprets his journey through the contrast between glory and suffering. The disciple who desired a place of honor had to learn a form of participation that included Christ's passion. This is a theological reading of the Gospel episodes, not a reconstruction of James's unrecorded thoughts or final speeches. Its force rests on comparing what the texts actually preserve.
james-the-greater.reflection: Read the request for places of honor and Acts 12:1–2 together. Discuss how the contrast changes an account of James that mentions only his closeness to Jesus.

jane-frances-de-chantal.title: Written guidance for a growing community
paragraphs: Jane's contribution survives in more than the story of the Visitation's foundation. Her writings include instructions on religious life, letters, responses concerning the order's rules and customs, and testimony for Francis de Sales's beatification process. These are different literary forms, each produced for a practical audience and purpose.

The scale of the community made such guidance consequential. The Catholic Encyclopedia records thirteen houses at Francis's death in 1622 and eighty-six by Jane's death in 1641. Written answers could help sisters in separate houses address shared questions, while her formal testimony preserved memories of her collaborator. Expansion required a means of communicating judgment as well as establishing buildings.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: Jane Frances de Chantal

jane-frances-de-chantal.reflection: Choose one practical question that a newly founded Visitation house might need to resolve. Discuss how a letter, a rule, and formal testimony would each address a different need.

januarius.title: The companions named with Naples' patron
paragraphs: The martyrological tradition names Januarius with Festus, Desiderius, Sossius, Proculus, Eutyches, and Acutius. It identifies several different ministries, including deacons and a reader, and associates the group with Benevento, Miseno, and Pozzuoli. Although the later accounts cannot establish every event, these names preserve a collective remembrance often overshadowed by Naples' most famous patron.

The Catholic Encyclopedia traces Bede's account to an earlier collection of martyr narratives and distinguishes that textual inheritance from the much later addition about liquefaction. Following those layers is more useful than treating the entire familiar story as one contemporary report. A named companion, an ancient martyrdom tradition, and a later relic observance are related but different subjects of study.
januarius.reflection: Make a list of Januarius's companions and the roles assigned to them in the martyrology. Discuss what disappears when a collective commemoration is told solely through its best-known figure.

jeanne-jugan.title: Hospitality learned through other religious traditions
paragraphs: The Little Sisters identify two particular influences on Jeanne's spirituality and working methods. From the teaching of John Eudes she learned to understand Christian life as continuing Christ's life and virtues. From the Brothers of Saint John of God she learned practical ways to seek donations for people in need.

The congregation also connects John of God's tradition with its fourth vow of hospitality. This gives a more precise institutional meaning to a word that can sound like ordinary friendliness. Hospitality became a sustained religious responsibility toward residents, supported by the participation of donors. Jeanne's work grew through receiving and adapting earlier examples, as well as through her own founding initiative.

sources.title: Little Sisters of the Poor: Jeanne Jugan

jeanne-jugan.reflection: Compare the influence of John Eudes with that of the Brothers of Saint John of God on Jeanne. Identify how a theological conviction and a practical method could reinforce one another.

jerome.title: A scholar who preserved other authors
paragraphs: Jerome's De viris illustribus presented the lives and works of more than a hundred Christian writers. Benedict XVI describes the project as a demonstration that Christian literature had developed a culture worthy of comparison with classical literature. Jerome was therefore a historian of writing as well as a translator of Scripture.

His approach to commentary also allowed room for a reader's judgment. He could set out several interpretations for comparison rather than conceal disagreement behind a single explanation. That method asks the reader to assess arguments and sources. It provides a useful counterpoint to his combative reputation: preserving alternatives and identifying earlier authors were themselves forms of intellectual service.
jerome.reflection: Read one entry from De viris illustribus and distinguish biographical information, a list of writings, and Jerome's judgment. Discuss how later readers benefit from each.

joachim.title: A commemoration with a changing calendar
paragraphs: Joachim's liturgical history illustrates how established devotion need not imply an unchanging feast date. The Catholic Encyclopedia records early Greek observance after Mary's birthday and several different dates in the Latin tradition. It also notes the restoration of his feast by Gregory XV in 1622 and its later placement by Clement XII in 1738.

These changes concern how communities organized public remembrance; they cannot establish a date in Joachim's otherwise undocumented personal life. The historical calendar is therefore a source for the reception of Mary's father, separate from the apocryphal narratives about him. Keeping those questions apart makes sense of older prayer books whose dates differ from the present shared commemoration of Joachim and Anne.
joachim.reflection: Find an older calendar entry for Joachim and compare it with the present July 26 commemoration. Explain why a changed feast date does not imply a changed historical birthday.

joan-of-arc.title: A dictated letter before the relief of Orléans
paragraphs: On March 22, 1429, Joan dictated a letter to the English king and the forces besieging Orléans. Benedict XVI discusses it as an appeal concerning peace and justice between two Christian peoples. The letter places her religious language within an explicit political address, before the city's relief in May.

Her later reception reached a very different setting in Thérèse of Lisieux's cloister. Benedict notes Thérèse's closeness to Joan's example and the Church's association of both women with French patronage. That connection is a history of interpretation, not evidence that their lives followed the same pattern. A military participant's remembered fidelity could become meaningful to a woman whose vocation unfolded within a monastery.
joan-of-arc.reflection: Compare the audience and purpose of Joan's 1429 letter with Thérèse's later interest in her. Discuss which elements of a life can be received across very different vocations.

john-baptist-de-la-salle.title: Why free schooling challenged established interests
paragraphs: The Brothers' history notes that De La Salle insisted on free schooling even for pupils whose families could have paid. That principle could bring his schools into conflict with established educational interests. The issue was therefore more specific than a general desire to assist poor children: it concerned how a school defined access and financed its common work.

The new community also consisted of consecrated laymen rather than an association of priests. Its teaching mission required a recognized form of religious life organized around shared responsibility for schools. These two commitments—gratuitous access and the brothers' collective vocation—help explain why educational reform brought institutional opposition as well as classroom innovation.

sources.title: Brothers of the Christian Schools: Founder

john-baptist-de-la-salle.reflection: Discuss the consequences of a school charging no pupil fees, including families able to pay. Connect that policy with De La Salle's effort to form a stable community of teachers.

john-baptist-de-rossi.title: The associations behind an accessible ministry
paragraphs: De Rossi's early formation included the Marian sodality and the Ristretto of the Twelve Apostles at the Roman College. The Catholic Encyclopedia describes him leading fellow members in visits to sick people and other works of mercy. Organized service thus formed part of his student years, before the better-known ministry of his priesthood.

His later move into hearing confessions also involved renewed study. After encouragement from the bishop at Cività Castellana, he reviewed moral theology before receiving permission to hear confessions across Rome's churches. The sequence joins personal encouragement with preparation and authorization. It shows pastoral accessibility developing through learning and institutional support, rather than goodwill alone.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: John Baptist de Rossi

john-baptist-de-rossi.reflection: Trace the sequence from De Rossi's student associations to his review of moral theology. Identify how companionship, study, and authorization each supported practical service.

john-berchmans.title: The public work of a student
paragraphs: Berchmans's final studies included formal public disputations. He was chosen to defend the philosophy course at the Roman College and then to represent it in another disputation at the Greek College. These were occasions on which a student had to explain and defend learning before others, not simply complete private reading.

The Jesuit account places those demands beside his worsening health and subsequent care in the infirmary. Fellow students visited, and the community brought him Communion in procession. His remembered fidelity therefore belongs within a shared academic and religious household. The account also leaves room to reflect critically on the demands placed on a capable student whose strength was declining.
john-berchmans.reflection: Compare private study with a public disputation, then discuss what Berchmans's illness adds to a conversation about achievement, responsibility, and care within a school.

john-bosco.title: The local history behind the Salesian name
paragraphs: The Salesians' account of their name includes the Marchioness Barolo, whose intended foundation at Turin was to have Francis de Sales as patron. When Bosco's oratory used premises connected with her work in 1844, that existing devotion joined his own admiration for Francis's gentleness. The name developed within concrete relationships of patronage and place.

The account also places Bosco's choice within Catholic controversies with the Waldensians. His Catholic Readings, begun in 1853, participated in that polemical setting. This historical context helps explain why Francis represented both pastoral kindness and a model of defending Catholic belief for Bosco. Understanding the setting need not reproduce the hostility of nineteenth-century religious disputes.

sources.title: Salesians of Don Bosco: Our origins and educational mission

john-bosco.reflection: Identify the different reasons the Salesian history gives for choosing Francis de Sales as patron. Discuss how a community's name can reflect local support, educational ideals, and the conflicts of its time.

john-cantius.title: A scholar's tomb as a place of encounter
paragraphs: John's tomb in the collegiate church of Saint Anne became a destination for people beyond the university where he had taught. The Chicago parish account also recalls John Paul II praying there during his 1997 visit to Poland, in connection with a gathering of university professors. The tomb linked a medieval teacher's memory with a later academic community.

His surviving manuscript work gives that remembrance material substance. The parish account describes twenty-six volumes totaling more than eighteen thousand pages. These are traces of repeated intellectual labor, not merely symbols attached after his death. Reading a copied page beside a later tribute distinguishes what John physically produced from the meanings subsequent generations found in his example.

sources.title: St. John Cantius Church: Patron biography

john-cantius.reflection: Consider a surviving manuscript volume and John Paul II's visit to John's tomb as two forms of evidence. Explain what each reveals about a teacher's legacy.

john-chrysostom.title: An urban vision drawn from Acts
paragraphs: In his preaching on Acts, Chrysostom treated the early Christians' sharing of possessions as a model for the life of a city. Benedict XVI interprets this as a demand reaching beyond occasional almsgiving toward the organization of common life. The needs of poor residents were therefore a question for the whole community, not only generous individuals.

His account of Scripture also used the image of a letter sent by God to humanity. Creation could point toward its Creator, while Scripture helped people understand that relationship more clearly. These themes connect his biblical interpretation with his social teaching: the text read in church was meant to shape how the city's inhabitants recognized and treated one another.
john-chrysostom.reflection: Read Acts 4:32–37 and distinguish an individual act of generosity from a shared arrangement for meeting needs. Use that distinction to discuss Chrysostom's urban ideal.

john-climacus.title: Redirecting desire rather than erasing it
paragraphs: Benedict XVI's reading of the Ladder emphasizes that human passions are not simply evil in themselves. Their moral direction depends on how they are used; disciplined desire can become energy for love of God. This distinction helps prevent John's demanding ascetic language from being reduced to hostility toward every feeling or human attachment.

Discernment is central to that transformation. The same outward action can arise from different motives, so the monk must examine what is happening within it. John's treatment of prayer likewise moves from bodily expressions toward prayer of the heart. The work concerns the formation of attention and desire, not merely the accumulation of difficult practices.
john-climacus.reflection: Choose an ordinary strong desire, such as the wish to excel. Using John's distinction, discuss how its direction and underlying motive could make it constructive or destructive.

john-de-br-beuf.title: Supplying a mission as well as teaching it
paragraphs: The Jesuit account records Brébeuf bringing twenty canoes of grain to Quebec in 1629, when an English blockade had interrupted French supplies. It also describes his responsibility for provisioning the mission between 1641 and 1644. These tasks place food, transport, and coordination alongside language learning in the practical history of his work.

The account of his return to Wendat country in 1634 supplies another revealing detail: an epidemic had reduced the visiting canoe fleet sharply, and hosts were reluctant to accept extra passengers. Their decisions affected when and how missionaries could travel. That dependence should remain visible when reading European narratives that otherwise place missionary initiative at the center of every event.

sources.title: Society of Jesus: Jean de Brébeuf

john-de-br-beuf.reflection: Compare Brébeuf's grain convoy with the smaller Wendat fleet described in 1634. Identify how food supply, illness, and decisions by Indigenous hosts shaped the mission's possibilities.

john-eudes.title: A second foundation for women seeking refuge
paragraphs: Eudes's institutional work also included a house at Caen for women seeking to leave prostitution, established in 1641 with assistance from members of the Company of the Blessed Sacrament. The project addressed a need he encountered in ministry that could not be met simply by improving the education of future priests.

He later entrusted this work to religious women, with help from the Visitation community at Caen. It developed into the Order of Our Lady of Charity, receiving episcopal and papal recognition. The sequence reveals several kinds of collaboration: supporters made an initial refuge possible, experienced religious women helped shape its life, and formal recognition gave the community a more durable institutional place.

sources.title: Eudists: John Eudes, foundations and spiritual legacy

john-eudes.reflection: Set Eudes's seminary and refuge foundations side by side. Discuss why two needs encountered in ministry required different communities, preparation, and forms of support.

john-fisher.title: Patronage that made learning possible
paragraphs: Fisher's educational influence included the Lady Margaret professorships of divinity at Oxford and Cambridge; he became the first holder of the Cambridge chair. His connection with Margaret Beaufort therefore supported teaching posts as well as college foundations. An endowed position could give theological study a continuing place beyond the career of one teacher.

He also encouraged Erasmus to come to Cambridge. The Catholic Encyclopedia points to Erasmus's acknowledgment of Fisher's protection for Greek studies there. This relationship adds a specific dimension to Fisher's reputation as a scholar: supporting another scholar and the study of a language could change the intellectual resources available to a whole university.
john-fisher.reflection: Compare founding a college with endowing a professorship and supporting a visiting scholar. Explain how Fisher's educational patronage operated at each of these levels.

john-francis-regis.title: How a French missionary became a college's patron
paragraphs: The institution now known as Regis University adopted his name in 1921. Its history explains that the earlier name, College of the Sacred Heart, had become awkward in sporting chants and newspaper coverage. President Robert Kelley sought a new name as part of a broader effort to strengthen the college's public identity.

The faculty considered Newman and Regis, and the board chose Regis after learning the Jesuit provincial's preference; the change took effect on July 1. This is a concrete example of a saint's later reception, with an institutional decision that can be dated and explained. It should be distinguished from a school founded personally by the saint, who had died centuries earlier in France.
john-francis-regis.reflection: Read the university's account of its 1921 name change. Discuss how choosing a patron can combine religious memory with the practical needs of a later institution.
